title: Schelling on New York
hook: Measure a random mix on New York's shape. What can the number say, and what can't it?

knows: the Schelling mechanism from the Economics lesson (a simple moving rule sorts a grid), though this card explains its own squares and rule
that cities can have neighbourhoods where one group is concentrated
doesNotKnow: that a segregation index depends on the size of the unit it is measured on (a random mix already scores about 0.4 to 0.5 on small blocks)
what a model like this can and cannot say about a real city

misconception: If a simple model reproduces a city's pattern, then that is why the city looks that way. Second: a mix placed at random would score a segregation index near zero.
objective: The learner can explain that an unevenness index such as D depends on the unit it is measured on (a random mix scores about 0.45 on 2 x 2-cell blocks and less on larger ones, and a census tract holds thousands of people), that in this toy model a simple moving rule sorts the grid to about 0.75, and that the model leaves out money, prices, jobs, history and who was allowed to live where, so it does not show why any real city looks as it does.

claims.text: The index of dissimilarity D measures how unevenly two groups are spread over a set of units, from 0 (both groups spread in the same proportions over every unit) to 1 (no unit holds both groups); it equals the share of one group that would have to change units for an even spread. On the card only as 'how unevenly spread (0 even, 1 fully apart)'; the 'would have to change units' gloss is in this claim only (cultural review R4).
claims.source: Massey, D. S. and Denton, N. A. (1988). The dimensions of residential segregation. Social Forces 67(2): 281-315 (evenness, index of dissimilarity). Computed in engine.ts dissimilarity(): D = 0.5 * sum over aligned k x k blocks of |a_i/A - b_i/B|, over agents only (walls and empty cells ignored). Builder: citation from memory, not opened (no egress). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14: VERIFIED. Citation (Social Forces 67(2): 281-315, 1988; evenness as one of five dimensions, indices surveyed per dimension) confirmed from search-indexed bibliographic and abstract listings only; the paper itself was not opened (publisher unreachable). Definition, endpoints and the 'would have to change units' gloss confirmed by derivation from the formula: 0 iff a_i/A = b_i/B in every unit, 1 iff no unit holds both; because the signed terms sum to 0, the positive part equals D, the share of one group to move for an even spread. engine.ts dissimilarity() re-implemented independently, same values. See company/reviews/schelling-on-new-york/2026-10-14-fact-check.md.

claims.text: In this model, two equal groups placed at random on the grid already score about 0.4 to 0.5 on blocks of 2 x 2 cells, before anyone moves.
claims.source: engine.ts run(seed, 30), frames[0], dissimilarity(frame, 40, 2). Builder run 2026-10-14 (node src/demos/geography/schelling-on-new-york/check.mjs): the lesson's seeds (1 to 50 without 3 and 36, 48 seeds) start at 0.42-0.53, mean 0.46; seed 1 (the default) 0.47. Seed 1 is simply the first seed, not chosen for its result; seeds 3 and 36 are left out of New mix because their settled frame leaves one region of the city more than 90% one group (edge artefact, cultural review R2), not for their D. Same rule as the brief's check script (check.mjs shows start frames, end frames and ticks identical for seeds 1 to 50). The stage and the reveal quote the learner's own start value. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14: VERIFIED. Re-ran check.mjs and the brief's script (equal50); independent re-implementation of D over engine frames: 48 lesson seeds start 0.421-0.525 (mean 0.461) on 2x2, all 259/259 agents; seed 1 0.47. Every seed rounds into 'about 0.4 to 0.5'. See company/reviews/schelling-on-new-york/2026-10-14-fact-check.md.

claims.text: In this model, at the 30% setting (move if fewer than 30% of occupied neighbouring cells hold the same group), the grid settles with everyone staying, and D on 2 x 2-cell blocks rises to about 0.75.
claims.source: engine.ts run(seed, 30). Builder run 2026-10-14 (check.mjs), the lesson's 48 seeds: settled D on 2 x 2 blocks 0.67-0.83, mean 0.75; all settle in 7-24 ticks; seed 1: 0.47 -> 0.76 in 7 ticks (matches the brief's real-mask numbers, company/domains/briefs/checks/nyc-mask-40.md). The reveal quotes the learner's own last settled 30% run, pinned on the stage when the reveal opens. Slider range 0-30% in steps of 5 (cultural review 2, ruling (a)): at 35% and above the settled frame can leave one region of the city more than 90% one group (35%: 2 of 48 seeds; 40%: 3; 45-50%: 4). check.mjs scans every frame of every lesson seed at every setting 0-30% (1,865 frames): no region (at least 10 agents) over 90% one group; worst 0.86. Every lesson seed settles at every setting 0-30% (max 24 ticks). The 'would stay' readout is floor(100 x (agents - movers) / agents) at the frame shown, so it reads 100% only when no square would move (check.mjs: 0 frames read 100% with movers, 0-30%). v2 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14): slider capped at 30% and readout changed from Math.round to an integer floor after the fact-check dispute; reset to unverified for re-check.

claims.text: D depends on the size of the unit it is measured on: the same model grid scores 1.00 on single cells (every cell holds one agent) and less on larger blocks; at the random start about 0.46 on 2 x 2, 0.26 on 4 x 4 and 0.14 on 8 x 8 cells, and after settling at 30% about 0.75, 0.53 and 0.33.
claims.source: engine.ts dissimilarity(frame, 40, k) for k = 1, 2, 4, 8 over the lesson's 48 seeds (check.mjs, 2026-10-14): start 1.00 / 0.42-0.53 (mean 0.46) / 0.21-0.31 (0.26) / 0.10-0.19 (0.14); settled at 30% 1.00 / 0.67-0.83 (0.75) / 0.44-0.64 (0.53) / 0.22-0.45 (0.33). Seed 1: start 1.00 / 0.47 / 0.27 / 0.12, settled 1.00 / 0.76 / 0.53 / 0.34. On the stage each block button the learner has pressed shows its value at the start and now; the reveal quotes the learner's run at 2 x 2 and the largest other block size they measured. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14: VERIFIED. Independent D re-implementation over the 48 lesson seeds: start 1.000 / 0.421-0.525 (0.461) / 0.212-0.309 (0.255) / 0.104-0.185 (0.138); settled 1.000 / 0.672-0.834 (0.753) / 0.436-0.637 (0.529) / 0.224-0.448 (0.330) for 1x1/2x2/4x4/8x8. Seed 1 values as stated; the walkthrough reveal (0.47, 0.12, 0.76) matches. See company/reviews/schelling-on-new-york/2026-10-14-fact-check.md.

claims.text: In this model, a simple moving rule sorts the grid: a simplified version of Thomas Schelling's segregation model.
claims.source: Simulation as in c6. Model: Schelling, T. C. (1971). Dynamic models of segregation. Journal of Mathematical Sociology 1(2): 143-186 (verified as a citation in economics.mild-preferences-sharp-divides.c6; the stage rule is the same simplified variant, moving to a random empty cell). Reworded per cultural review R3: 'a simple moving rule', not 'preferences'. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14: VERIFIED. Simulation as c6 (the sorting itself reproduces). Schelling 1971 citation rests on economics.mild-preferences-sharp-divides.c6 (verified 2026-10-14, secondary records). engine.ts reproduces abm.ts frame for frame on an all-land mask (check.mjs), so 'simplified version' carries over. See company/reviews/schelling-on-new-york/2026-10-14-fact-check.md.

claims.text: This model does not show why any real city looks as it does.
claims.source: Judgement about the model's scope (cultural review R3, brief claim 9): the rule has no money, prices, jobs, history or rules about who may live where (see c14), both groups follow the same rule and may move anywhere, and the grid is not a map of people (c12). Shown in the reveal, in the same paragraph as the model's result. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14: VERIFIED (scope judgement). Read engine.ts: inputs are only mask, empty share, two equal groups, seed and threshold; agents move to any empty cell at no cost. A model with none of the causes listed in c14 cannot show why a real city looks as it does. The card's wording ('does not show') stays within that. See company/reviews/schelling-on-new-york/2026-10-14-fact-check.md.

claims.text: Late-1930s US government maps graded neighbourhoods in US cities for lending risk.
claims.source: Mapping Inequality: Redlining in New Deal America, University of Richmond Digital Scholarship Lab, https://dsl.richmond.edu/panorama/redlining/ (the Home Owners' Loan Corporation maps, security grades A-D). Its area-description data (github.com/americanpanorama/HOLC_Area_Description_Data) date most surveys 1937-1939; New York City's map is 1938, so the card says 'late-1930s'. On the card, inside the sentence that begins 'In US cities': 'late-1930s government maps grading neighbourhoods for lending risk'. No acronym, no neighbourhood named beside a grade (R7). v2 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14): split from v1 c10a into c10a (this, Mapping Inequality only), c10d (Aaronson et al. 2021) and c10e (Fishback et al. 2024), one source each, after the fact-check dispute; '1938' changed to 'late-1930s'. Builder: Mapping Inequality site not opened (no egress).

claims.text: The maps' grades are associated with later outcomes in the graded neighbourhoods, such as home values and home ownership.
claims.source: Aaronson, D., Hartley, D. and Mazumder, B. (2021). The effects of the 1930s HOLC 'redlining' maps. American Economic Journal: Economic Policy 13(4): 355-392 (later home ownership, house values, rents and segregation by grade). The authors argue for an effect; the card states only an association, which understates the source. The card says outcomes, not lending: on the card 'The grades are associated with later home values and ownership'. v2 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14): split from v1 c10a after the fact-check dispute ('lending' was the authors' inferred mechanism, not a measured outcome). Builder: paper not opened (no egress).

claims.text: Research is mixed on whether the maps caused these later differences or recorded lending practice that already existed.
claims.source: Fishback, P., Rose, J., Snowden, K. and Storrs, T. (2024). New Evidence on Redlining by Federal Housing Programs in the 1930s. Journal of Urban Economics 141: 103462 (NBER Working Paper w29244, 2021): exclusion of such neighbourhoods by federal programmes predates the maps, and the maps had little effect on lending; set against Aaronson et al. (c10d), which finds an effect. On the card: 'research is mixed on whether the maps caused this or recorded earlier practice'. v2 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14): split from v1 c10a after the fact-check dispute (the 'mixed' clause needs its own source). Builder: paper not opened (no egress); the date is 2024 (journal) / 2021 (NBER), not 2022 as in R7.

claims.text: In US cities, households did not all have the same choices: the documented history includes housing and lending discrimination, which widened wealth gaps between groups.
claims.source: Rothstein, R. (2017). The Color of Law: A Forgotten History of How Our Government Segregated America. New York: Liveright (federal, state and local housing and lending discrimination; its effect on home equity and so on wealth). On the card: 'In US cities, households did not all have the same choices: the documented history includes housing and lending discrimination, widening wealth gaps, ...'. v2 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14): narrowed from 'income and wealth gaps' to 'wealth gaps' after the fact-check note (Rothstein's income argument runs partly the other way). Income is no longer on the card. Builder: book not opened (no egress); fact-checker, please find the page for the wealth/home-equity argument.

claims.text: Income and wealth differences between groups are part of the documented history of where households live.
claims.source: NYU Furman Center, State of New York City's Housing and Neighborhoods (annual report), https://furmancenter.org/stateofthecity (income differences across New York City neighbourhoods and groups). Builder: not opened (no egress). The card names income after discrimination and does not present it as a separate neutral cause (R3). Fact-checker: confirm the report covers income by group, or name a better single source. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14: DISPUTED. The named source cannot carry the text. Per search-indexed listings (furmancenter.org unreachable), the Furman Center State of the City citywide tables give New York City median household income by race and ethnicity (present-day). They do not cover wealth, and they are not a 'documented history of where households live'. Also, the card has no separate sentence for this claim: its only income/wealth words are 'then income and wealth gaps it widened', which c10b carries. Fix (builder): either withdraw c10c and let c10b carry 'income and wealth gaps', or keep it as an income-only claim ('income differs between groups in New York City') sourced to a named Furman Center edition and table, and source wealth separately (e.g. the Federal Reserve Survey of Consumer Finances). See company/reviews/schelling-on-new-york/2026-10-14-fact-check.md. | WITHDRAWN 2026-10-14 (demo-builder, v2): per the fact-check, the Furman Center tables are present-day NYC income by group, not a documented history, and do not cover wealth. The card no longer has an income clause; the only remaining wealth words ('widening wealth gaps') are carried by c10b (Rothstein 2017). No learner-visible text depends on this claim.

claims.text: The grid's shape comes from New York City's official city boundaries, rasterised to 40 x 40 cells of about 1.2 km (576 land cells).
claims.source: NYC Department of City Planning, Borough Boundaries, BYTES of the BIG APPLE release 16A (2016), nybb.shp, EPSG:2263; obtained from the PyPI wheel geopandas-0.14.4-py3-none-any.whl (geopandas/datasets/nybb_16a.zip, sha256 b4a98fc3b77be5af58676de9560c2782b902b83d1d8c7914dea8d0e75177e2a1), downloaded 2026-10-14 because the NYC Open Data host was unreachable; rasterised by company/domains/briefs/checks/nyc-mask-rasterise.mjs (cell centres, even-odd point-in-polygon, cell 3,855 ft); output company/domains/briefs/checks/nyc-mask-40.json, documented in nyc-mask-40.md. The lesson inlines only the 200-byte land bitmask (engine.ts MASK_HEX); no region labels reach the lesson (R2). check.mjs confirms MASK_HEX equals the JSON's land cells. v2 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14): claim text says 'city boundaries' (cultural review 2, advisory); the dataset is still the DCP Borough Boundaries file named above. Text change only; reset to unverified for re-check.

claims.text: A toy model on a grid shaped like New York City; two made-up equal groups; not a map of people and not a cause. The 30% setting is a setting in this model, not a measure of anyone.
claims.source: Judgement about the model (cultural review R9, R1, R6). On the stage (v2 wording, trimmed for the stage word budget per cultural review 2 (b)): 'Made-up equal groups, A and B. Not New York's population.' and, directly above the slider, 'A setting, not a measure of anyone.' Density is equal everywhere in the model (one agent per land cell, 10% empty) while real density varies. v2 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14): stage lines reworded; reset to unverified for re-check.

claims.text: In this model, a random mix scores about 0.4 to 0.5 on 2 x 2 blocks: a 2 x 2 block holds at most 4 squares, so chance alone makes blocks uneven, and the same mix scores lower on larger blocks. So a segregation number depends on its unit and means little without it.
claims.source: Recall card (R10). Restates c5 and c7 (48 lesson seeds: start 0.42-0.53 on 2 x 2, about 0.26 on 4 x 4, 0.14 on 8 x 8); 'squares', not 'households' (c12); one range, 0.4 to 0.5, in the question and here. Carries no real-city figure and no group names. v2 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14): reworded after the fact-check dispute; reset to unverified.

claims.text: Not modelled: money, prices, jobs, history, who could live where.
claims.source: Scope of the rule (engine.ts): the only inputs are the city mask, the share of empty cells, the two equal groups, the seed and the threshold; agents move to any empty cell at no cost. Shown on the stage after the learner's first finished run (R3 item 5); the reveal repeats part of it ('Without money or history, the model does not show why any real city looks as it does'). v2 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14): stage line trimmed per cultural review 2 (b) item 4 ('who could live where' for 'who was allowed to live where'); reset to unverified.

claims.text: A census tract holds thousands of people. A 2 x 2 block in this grid holds at most 4 squares.
claims.source: Tract size: US Census Bureau, Glossary, 'Census Tract' (https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/geography/about/glossary.html), which gives tracts generally between 1,200 and 8,000 people, optimum about 4,000 (builder: from memory, not opened). Grid block: derivation, a 2 x 2 block holds at most 4 cells, each at most one square. On the card: 'A census tract holds thousands of people; a 2×2 block here, at most 4 squares.' v2 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14): tied to the 2 x 2 block after the fact-check dispute ('a handful' was false for 8 x 8); 'census' added (cultural review 2). Reset to unverified.

recall.question: In this model, a random mix scores about 0.4 to 0.5 on 2 × 2 blocks. What does that tell you about a segregation number?
options: It depends on the unit it is measured on, so the unit must be stated
The random mix is already half sorted before anyone has moved
The number is broken, so it should not be used at all
recall.why: A 2 × 2 block holds at most 4 squares, so chance alone makes blocks uneven. The same mix scores lower on larger blocks. A number without its unit says little.
